proposedTopics.title: Foundry
proposedTopics.description: Foundry (forge/cast/anvil/chisel) is the primary toolchain for this curriculum: Solidity-native tests, fuzzing, invariants, scripting, and gas/coverage tooling, all without leaving Solidity. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/introduction/getting-started

proposedTopics.title: Hardhat 3
proposedTopics.description: Hardhat 3 is the secondary toolchain: TypeScript-first deploy pipelines (Ignition), network/config management, plugins, and Foundry-compatible Solidity tests, used where a typed JS/frontend workflow matters. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/getting-started

proposedTopics.title: Foundry project anatomy
proposedTopics.description: forge init scaffolds src/ (contracts), test/ (.t.sol tests), lib/ (dependencies), and script/ (deploy/interaction scripts); foundry.toml declares which directories those are and out/ holds the compiled artifacts (ABI + bytecode) forge build regenerates. Every other Foundry feature — remappings, profiles, gas snapshots — hooks into this layout, so knowing it is the entry point to the whole tool. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/introduction/getting-started
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in web3-practice (already scaffolded), confirm the src/test/lib/script/out layout matches foundry.toml's src/test/out/libs keys and write contracts/phase03/anatomy.md listing each directory's purpose. Done when: `forge build` succeeds and anatomy.md maps every foundry.toml path key to its directory.

proposedTopics.title: cast: chain interaction CLI
proposedTopics.description: cast is Foundry's terminal tool for reading and writing chain state without writing a script: call/send/balance/storage/logs/abi-encode against any RPC. It's the fastest way to sanity-check a deployed contract or decode a transaction. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/cast/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: against a local anvil, deploy a contract from contracts/phase03/ and run `cast call`, `cast send`, and `cast storage` on it, recording the three commands and their output in contracts/phase03/cast-notes.md. Done when: cast call returns the expected return value and cast storage reads a known slot.

proposedTopics.title: anvil: local test node
proposedTopics.description: anvil is a local, disposable Ethereum node with pre-funded accounts, instant mining, and cheat-friendly RPC extensions (anvil_setBalance, snapshot/revert) — the backbone of fast iterative testing and the target for scripts and fork-testing alike. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/anvil/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: start `anvil`, deploy a contract from contracts/phase03/ with `forge create`, then call `anvil_setBalance` via `cast rpc` on an account, recording the sequence in contracts/phase03/anvil-notes.md. Done when: `cast balance` confirms the balance change after the RPC call.

proposedTopics.title: chisel: Solidity REPL
proposedTopics.description: chisel is an interactive Solidity shell: type an expression or statement and see its result immediately, with full access to cheatcodes — faster than a full build/test cycle for checking a one-line assembly or ABI idea. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/chisel/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in `chisel`, evaluate `keccak256(abi.encodePacked("test"))` and one cheatcode call (e.g. `vm.addr(1)`), pasting both transcripts into contracts/phase03/chisel-notes.md. Done when: the transcript shows chisel resolving both without a full forge build.

proposedTopics.title: Unit testing with forge-std
proposedTopics.description: Foundry tests are Solidity contracts inheriting forge-std's Test, using setUp() for fixtures and functions prefixed test for cases; assertions (assertEq, assertTrue, …) give readable failure diffs. Each test runs against its own isolated EVM snapshot, so state never leaks between tests. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/forge/testing
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write test/phase03/Counter.t.sol testing a small Counter contract in contracts/phase03/Counter.sol, with setUp() deploying it and ≥2 test functions using assertEq. Done when: `forge test --match-path test/phase03/Counter.t.sol` passes both cases.

proposedTopics.title: Cheatcodes: prank & deal
proposedTopics.description: vm.prank(addr) makes the next external call appear to originate from addr (vm.startPrank/stopPrank covers a range of calls), and vm.deal(addr, amount) sets an address's ETH balance directly — together they let a test impersonate any caller and fund it without a real transaction. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/reference/cheatcodes/overview
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in test/phase03/Prank.t.sol, use vm.prank to call an onlyOwner-style function as a non-owner and assert it reverts, then vm.deal an address and assert its new balance. Done when: forge test passes and proves both the impersonation and the balance set.

proposedTopics.title: Cheatcodes: expectRevert & expectEmit
proposedTopics.description: vm.expectRevert(...) asserts the very next call reverts with a specific reason/selector/custom error, and vm.expectEmit(...) asserts the next call emits an event matching the topics/data declared beforehand — both turn "it should fail/emit" into a checkable assertion instead of a try/catch. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/reference/cheatcodes/overview
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in test/phase03/ExpectRevertEmit.t.sol, assert a custom-error revert with vm.expectRevert(MyError.selector) and assert an event with vm.expectEmit before a Transfer-style emit. Done when: forge test passes, and temporarily deleting either cheatcode line makes the test wrongly pass or fail, proving each is load-bearing.

proposedTopics.title: Cheatcodes: warp & roll
proposedTopics.description: vm.warp(timestamp) sets block.timestamp and vm.roll(number) sets block.number for the rest of the test, letting you jump a vesting schedule forward or simulate blocks passing without waiting in real time. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/reference/cheatcodes/overview
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in test/phase03/TimeTravel.t.sol, write a small vesting-style contract in contracts/phase03/ that unlocks after a timestamp, then use vm.warp to jump past it and assert the unlock succeeds. Done when: forge test passes and fails if the vm.warp call is removed.

proposedTopics.title: Fuzz testing
proposedTopics.description: A fuzz test takes typed parameters instead of none; Foundry generates hundreds of pseudo-random inputs (biased toward edge cases like 0 and type max) per run, executing --fuzz-runs times and shrinking any failing input to a minimal repro. It checks a property across an input space instead of one hand-picked example. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/forge/fuzz-testing
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write test/phase03/Fuzz.t.sol with `function testFuzz_Deposit(uint96 amount) public` on a contract in contracts/phase03/ asserting a deposit's recorded balance always equals amount. Done when: `forge test --fuzz-runs 256` passes, and a deliberately-broken version of the function fails with a shrunk counterexample.

proposedTopics.title: Fork testing
proposedTopics.description: Fork testing runs a test against a pinned snapshot of live chain state (vm.createFork / --fork-url), so you can call real deployed contracts (a DEX, an oracle) exactly as they exist on mainnet or an L2, cheaply and deterministically by pinning a block number. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/guides/fork-testing
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write test/phase03/Fork.t.sol that forks a public mainnet RPC at a pinned block and asserts a known ERC-20's totalSupply() at that block. Done when: `forge test --match-path test/phase03/Fork.t.sol --fork-url <rpc>` passes, and passes identically on a second run because the block is pinned.

proposedTopics.title: Invariant testing
proposedTopics.description: An invariant test declares a property that must hold after any sequence of calls (e.g. "total shares never exceed total supply"); Foundry's fuzzer drives a handler contract through random call sequences and checks the invariant after each, catching bugs that only appear after a specific multi-step history no unit test would think to write. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/guides/invariant-testing
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write test/phase03/Invariant.t.sol with a Handler contract wrapping deposit/withdraw on a contract in contracts/phase03/, and an invariant_totalAssetsMatchSum() asserting tracked balances sum to the contract's total. Done when: `forge test --match-path test/phase03/Invariant.t.sol` runs the configured depth/runs and the invariant holds.

proposedTopics.title: Debugging: traces & the interactive debugger
proposedTopics.description: -vvvv prints a full call trace (every internal call, event, and revert reason) for a failing test, turning "test failed" into "here's exactly which call and line reverted" instead of a single assertion message. For a step-by-step look, `forge test --debug <testFunctionName>` (or `forge script <path> --debug`) launches Foundry's interactive TUI debugger — step opcode-by-opcode with n/s/o, jump to start/end with g/G — showing source, stack, memory, storage, and call stack live at each step. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/forge/debugging
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: intentionally break a test in test/phase03/ (e.g. a wrong assert value), run `forge test -vvvv` on it and paste the relevant trace lines into contracts/phase03/debugging-notes.md explaining which frame reverted; then run `forge test --debug <testFunctionName>` on the same test and note which interactive command (n/s/o/g/G) you used to step to the reverting opcode. Done when: debugging-notes.md documents both the trace-based diagnosis and at least one interactive-debugger navigation command, then the test is fixed and passes.

proposedTopics.title: Gas snapshots
proposedTopics.description: forge snapshot records each test's gas usage into .gas-snapshot, and forge snapshot --check fails the build if a later change regresses gas beyond it — turning "did my refactor cost more gas" into an automated, committed baseline instead of a manual before/after. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/forge/gas-tracking
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `forge snapshot` after writing a function in contracts/phase03/, then deliberately regress its gas and run `forge snapshot --check`. Done when: the check fails on the regression and passes again after reverting the change.

proposedTopics.title: Coverage
proposedTopics.description: forge coverage instruments the bytecode to report line/branch/function coverage per contract, surfacing untested paths (an unreached else, a revert branch no test hits) that a simple "tests pass" summary can hide. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/reference/forge/coverage
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `forge coverage` on contracts/phase03/, identify one uncovered branch, then add a test that covers it. Done when: `forge coverage` shows that branch as covered and the overall report improves.

proposedTopics.title: Scripting & deployment (forge script)
proposedTopics.description: A Foundry script is a Solidity contract with a run() function that uses vm.startBroadcast()/stopBroadcast() to mark which calls become real signed transactions when run with --broadcast; without that flag it's a dry-run simulation against a fork, making deploy scripts themselves testable before they touch a real chain. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/forge/scripting
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write script/Phase03Deploy.s.sol deploying a contract from contracts/phase03/ inside startBroadcast/stopBroadcast, then run it against a local anvil with and without --broadcast. Done when: the dry run and the broadcast run both succeed, and `cast code <addr>` confirms the deployed bytecode.

proposedTopics.title: Contract verification
proposedTopics.description: forge verify-contract uploads your source, compiler settings, and constructor args to a block explorer's API so it can recompile and compare against your deployed bytecode: identical including the trailing metadata hash is a "full match"; identical except that hash (e.g. compiled with bytecode_hash = "none") is still accepted as a "partial match" — either way turning an opaque deployed contract into human-readable, trust-minimized source on Etherscan/Blockscout/Sourcify. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/reference/forge/verify-contract, 📖 https://docs.sourcify.dev/blog/talk-about-onchain-metadata-hash/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase03/verify-notes.md, write the exact forge verify-contract command (address, chain, constructor-args encoding) you would run for the contract deployed by script/Phase03Deploy.s.sol on a public testnet, and state whether the project's bytecode_hash setting would produce a full or partial match. Done when: the notes correctly encode constructor args with `cast abi-encode`, name the required --etherscan-api-key, and correctly classify the expected match type.

proposedTopics.title: Dependency management: git submodules
proposedTopics.description: forge install <org/repo> adds a dependency as a git submodule under lib/, pinned to a commit — Foundry's classic default. Dependencies are vendored source you can read and diff, but the submodule state (.gitmodules + the pinned commit) must travel with the repo or a fresh clone gets empty lib/ folders. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/projects/dependencies
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `forge install OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts` in web3-practice and record the resulting lib/ entry and .gitmodules line in contracts/phase03/deps.md. Done when: `forge build` resolves an import from the installed dependency and deps.md explains why `git submodule update --init` is needed after a fresh clone.

proposedTopics.title: remappings.txt & import resolution
proposedTopics.description: remappings.txt (or remappings in foundry.toml) rewrites Solidity import prefixes to real paths — e.g. @openzeppelin/=lib/openzeppelin-contracts/ — so contracts import a short stable prefix instead of a long relative lib/ path; forge remappings prints the FULL resolved table, including entries auto-inferred from installed dependencies you never wrote by hand. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/reference/forge/remappings
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: add an explicit remapping in remappings.txt for the dependency installed in the git-submodules leaf, update an import in contracts/phase03/ to use the short prefix, and run `forge remappings` to confirm it resolves. Done when: `forge build` compiles the short-prefixed import and `forge remappings` lists your line.

proposedTopics.title: soldeer package manager
proposedTopics.description: soldeer is Foundry's newer registry-based package manager (forge soldeer install <pkg>~<version>) — an alternative to git submodules that resolves versioned releases from a central registry into dependencies/ and writes a [dependencies] entry into foundry.toml, closer to npm/cargo than to vendored git history. It coexists with submodule-based deps in the same project. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/projects/soldeer
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `forge soldeer install @openzeppelin-contracts~5.0.0` (or the current pinned version) in web3-practice and record the [dependencies] entry it writes to foundry.toml in contracts/phase03/deps.md, contrasting it with the submodule entry from the git-submodules leaf. Done when: `forge build` resolves an import from the soldeer-installed package.

proposedTopics.title: foundry.toml profiles
proposedTopics.description: foundry.toml supports named [profile.X] blocks (default is [profile.default]) that override any setting — FOUNDRY_PROFILE=ci forge test picks up [profile.ci]'s higher fuzz-run count without touching the fast default local settings. One config file drives both a quick local loop and a thorough CI check. Resources: 📖 https://getfoundry.sh/config/profiles
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in web3-practice's foundry.toml, confirm/extend the [profile.ci] block to raise fuzz.runs above the default, then compare the fuzz-run count in `forge test` output between `FOUNDRY_PROFILE=ci forge test` and a default run. Done when: the ci-profile run visibly performs more fuzz runs than the default profile on the same test.

proposedTopics.title: Static analysis: Slither & Aderyn wiring
proposedTopics.description: Slither (Python, mature, dozens of detectors) and Aderyn (Rust, Foundry-native, fast) both parse contracts without executing them, flagging patterns like reentrancy-prone external calls, unchecked-return values, or uninitialized state before a single test runs — catching bug classes a test suite only catches if someone thought to test for them. Resources: 🔗 https://github.com/crytic/slither, 🔗 https://github.com/Cyfrin/aderyn
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: install and run `slither .` (or `aderyn .`) against contracts/phase03/ in web3-practice, recording its findings in contracts/phase03/static-analysis.md with one detector class each tool caught named explicitly. Done when: the tool runs to completion against the repo and static-analysis.md names at least one specific detector.

proposedTopics.title: Hardhat 3 project setup
proposedTopics.description: A Hardhat 3 project is a Node/TS package with hardhat.config.ts at its root declaring the Solidity version, paths, and networks; npx hardhat --init scaffolds it, and Hardhat 3 ships Foundry-compatible Solidity tests as a first-class option alongside its original TypeScript test runner. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/getting-started
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: confirm web3-practice's hardhat.config.ts compiles the same contracts/ tree Foundry uses, then run `npx hardhat build`. Done when: hardhat build succeeds against the shared contracts/ directory with no config errors.

proposedTopics.title: TypeScript testing with viem
proposedTopics.description: Hardhat's TS tests pair hardhat-toolbox-viem with a test runner: you get a typed viem client per network, deploy contracts via a viem.deployContract helper, and assert with viem's typed read/write calls — useful for testing deploy-time wiring and multi-contract integration the same way a frontend would call it. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/guides/testing/using-viem
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write a TS test in test/ deploying a contract from contracts/phase03/ via the viem helper and asserting a read call's typed return value. Done when: `npx hardhat test` passes the TS suite.

proposedTopics.title: Hardhat Ignition deployment
proposedTopics.description: Ignition is Hardhat's declarative deployment system: a module describes contracts and their constructor/dependency graph (not imperative steps), and Ignition figures out the order, tracks what's already been deployed in a journal, and can safely resume a partially-failed deploy without redeploying what already succeeded. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/guides/deployment/using-ignition
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write deploy/Phase03Module.ts as an Ignition module deploying a contract from contracts/phase03/ (with a constructor arg), then run `npx hardhat ignition deploy deploy/Phase03Module.ts --network localhost`. Done when: the deployment succeeds and re-running the same command is a no-op because Ignition's journal recognizes it's already deployed.

proposedTopics.title: Network & config management
proposedTopics.description: hardhat.config.ts's networks object maps a name to either an in-memory simulated network (edr-simulated, with optional forking) or a real JSON-RPC endpoint (http, with url/accounts); --network <name> on any Hardhat command selects which one runs, and configuration variables keep secrets like RPC URLs out of the committed config. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/reference/configuration
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: add an http-style network entry to web3-practice's hardhat.config.ts using a configuration variable for the RPC URL (no hardcoded secret), and a forking entry pointed at a public mainnet RPC. Done when: the forking network starts and a read call confirms it's forking the intended chain's state.

proposedTopics.title: Hardhat plugins ecosystem
proposedTopics.description: Almost all of Hardhat's functionality beyond core compile/run is a plugin (hardhat-toolbox-viem bundles the common set: viem, Ignition, gas reporting, verification); plugins register new tasks, config keys, and extensions to the Hardhat Runtime Environment every task/script receives, so picking the right plugin set is how a project assembles its actual capabilities. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/plugins/official-plugins
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: list, in contracts/phase03/plugins.md, every plugin web3-practice's hardhat.config.ts currently imports and the one capability each adds (e.g. viem client, Ignition, gas stats). Done when: the list matches the actual imports in hardhat.config.ts and names each plugin's added task or config key.

proposedTopics.title: Coexisting: shared remappings + .t.sol tests
proposedTopics.description: Hardhat 3 does NOT parse foundry.toml — it loads its own remappings.txt files instead (found at the project root, in subdirectories, or bundled inside an installed npm package), and treats npm packages and git submodules alike as Solidity dependencies. What the two tools genuinely share is the .t.sol test format: Hardhat 3 ships Foundry-compatible Solidity tests natively, so any test/ file or file ending .t.sol written against forge-std runs under `npx hardhat test` unchanged. Two separate configs, one compatible remapping convention and one shared test format. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/guides/writing-contracts/remappings, 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/guides/testing/using-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in web3-practice, add a remappings.txt entry at the project root for the dependency installed in the git-submodules leaf, then compile and run the SAME test/phase03/*.t.sol file under both `forge test` and `npx hardhat test`. Done when: both tools resolve the remapped import and both run the identical .t.sol file — proving Hardhat needs its own remappings.txt (not foundry.toml) and that its Solidity test runner accepts an unmodified Foundry-style test.

proposedTopics.title: Shared artifacts & mixed test suites
proposedTopics.description: Because Hardhat 3's own Solidity test runner recognizes the same .t.sol/forge-std test files Foundry uses, one project can run a test file under `forge test` for Foundry's fuzzer/invariant/gas tooling AND run the identical file under `npx hardhat test`, plus separate Hardhat TS tests for deployment/integration coverage — all against one shared contracts/ tree, with no test forked per tool. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/guides/testing/using-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run the SAME test/phase03/*.t.sol file (e.g. the Counter test from the Unit testing with forge-std leaf) under both `forge test` and `npx hardhat test` in web3-practice, without editing the test file between runs. Done when: both commands exit 0 running the identical .t.sol file in the same working tree.

proposedTopics.title: When to reach for Foundry vs Hardhat
proposedTopics.description: Foundry wins for fast, deep testing (fuzz/invariant/gas/security work all live in Solidity, iterating in milliseconds); Hardhat wins when rich TypeScript tooling matters — typed deploy pipelines via Ignition, viem/wagmi frontend integration, or JS-ecosystem plugins. Because both can already run the same .t.sol tests against one contracts/ tree, most real repos use both: Foundry for the fast local test loop, Hardhat for deployment and anything touching a frontend. Resources: 📖 https://hardhat.org/docs/hardhat3/whats-new
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase03/tooling-decision.md, write a one-paragraph decision rule for web3-practice's later phases — which phases' Builds will run under `forge test` vs `npx hardhat ignition deploy` — and why, noting that both tools can already run the same .t.sol tests from the Shared artifacts leaf. Done when: the rule names at least one concrete upcoming phase for each tool.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do src/, test/, lib/, script/, and out/ each hold in a Foundry project, and which one is safe to delete/regenerate?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: src/ = contracts, test/ = .t.sol tests, lib/ = installed dependencies (submodules/soldeer), script/ = deploy/interaction scripts, out/ = build artifacts (ABI+bytecode). Pitfall: out/ is a build cache regenerated by forge build — never hand-edit it, and it's normally gitignored.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Name three things cast can do without writing a Solidity script, and why cast call can never change state.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: cast call (read), cast send (write tx), cast storage (raw slot read), plus abi-encode/logs/etc. — all from the terminal against any RPC. Pitfall: cast call behaves like eth_call — it never actually mines a tx, even against a live node, so it can't be used to change state.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes anvil faster to iterate against than a public testnet, and what happens to its state on restart?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Instant mining, pre-funded rich accounts, and cheat-friendly RPC extensions (anvil_setBalance, snapshot/revert) for cheap state resets. Pitfall: anvil's state is ephemeral by default — restart it and everything (deployed contracts, balances) is gone unless you pass --state or dump/load it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is chisel faster than forge test for checking a one-line Solidity/assembly idea, and what does it share with real tests?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It evaluates each statement immediately in an interactive session instead of a full compile+run cycle, with full access to Foundry cheatcodes just like a test. Pitfall: a working chisel snippet doesn't automatically become a committed test — copy it into a real test file.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does each Foundry test function run against its own isolated EVM state, and what does that mean for relying on test execution order?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Every test* function gets setUp() re-run and a fresh state snapshot, so tests can't leak state into each other regardless of order. Pitfall: a test that depends on state created by an earlier test's body (not its own setUp()) will break — each test only sees its own setUp() plus its own body.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a minimal Foundry test file skeleton testing a Counter contract's increment().
proposedPrompts.answerHint: import {Test} from "forge-std/Test.sol"; import {Counter} from "../src/Counter.sol"; contract CounterTest is Test { Counter c; function setUp() public { c = new Counter(); } function test_Increment() public { c.increment(); assertEq(c.count(), 1); } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What's the difference between vm.prank and vm.startPrank/stopPrank, and what does vm.deal NOT do?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: prank affects only the next external call; startPrank/stopPrank affects every call until stopPrank. vm.deal sets a balance directly — it runs no real transfer logic (no receive/fallback triggered). Pitfall: forgetting stopPrank leaves impersonation active for later, unrelated calls in the same test.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write cheatcode calls making the next call appear from address(0xBEEF) with a 10 ether balance.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: vm.deal(address(0xBEEF), 10 ether); vm.prank(address(0xBEEF)); target.doSomething();

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where must vm.expectRevert/vm.expectEmit be placed relative to the call they check, and what's the risk of a bare vm.expectRevert() with no arguments?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Immediately before the call being tested — the cheatcode applies only to the very next external call. Pitfall: vm.expectRevert() with no args matches ANY revert reason, which can hide a wrong-reason bug — pass the specific selector/string when you can.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do vm.warp and vm.roll each control, and does setting one automatically advance the other?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: vm.warp(ts) sets block.timestamp; vm.roll(n) sets block.number — instantly, for all subsequent calls in the test. Pitfall: warping doesn't advance block.number and vice versa; a contract checking both may need both cheatcodes set consistently.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Foundry do when a fuzz test fails, and why does fuzzing catch bugs example-based unit tests often miss?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It shrinks the failing input to a minimal counterexample and reports it. Fuzzing explores many inputs (including edge values like 0 and type max) per run instead of the few a human thinks to write. Pitfall: fuzz inputs need explicit bounds (bound()/vm.assume()) or many runs are wasted on invalid inputs that get discarded.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a fuzz test asserting a Vault's deposit always credits the exact amount deposited.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function testFuzz_Deposit(uint96 amount) public { vm.assume(amount > 0); vault.deposit{value: amount}(); assertEq(vault.balanceOf(address(this)), amount); }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does pinning a fork to a specific block number matter for test determinism?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Without a pinned block, forking 'latest' means the exact state (balances, oracle prices) differs run to run, so a passing test today could fail tomorrow for reasons unrelated to your code. Pitfall: forking without a rate-limit-safe RPC can hit limits mid-suite — use a dedicated fork RPC or cache.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is a 'handler' in Foundry invariant testing, and what does it catch that a single fuzz test doesn't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A handler wraps the target's functions with bounded/valid inputs; the fuzzer calls handler functions in random sequences and order, then checks the invariant after each — catching bugs that only surface after a specific multi-call history. Pitfall: an unconstrained handler wastes runs on reverting calls — bound inputs inside the handler, not just the invariant.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does -vvvv add to `forge test` output that a plain failing assertion message doesn't tell you?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A full call trace: every internal/external call, its arguments, emitted events, and the exact revert reason/frame — so you see WHERE in a call chain something reverted. Pitfall: trace verbosity is expensive on invariant/fuzz runs — use it to debug one failing case, not as a default for the whole suite.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you launch Foundry's interactive debugger for one specific test, and what's the difference between the 's' and 'o' navigation commands once inside it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: `forge test --debug <testFunctionName>` (or `forge script <path> --debug` for scripts) opens the TUI debugger. 's' steps into the next call (goes a frame deeper into the call stack); 'o' steps out of the current call (back up a frame) — letting you drill into or skip past a sub-call while watching stack/memory/storage update live. Pitfall: --debug is invoked with a specific test function name, not a whole file — it opens one interactive run per invocation, not a batch view over the suite.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does `forge snapshot --check` actually fail the build on, and what must you do after an intentional gas increase?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It diffs the current run's gas-per-test against the committed .gas-snapshot file and fails if it changed. Pitfall: an intentional increase (e.g. added a safety check) needs .gas-snapshot regenerated and committed, or every future CI run fails on that line forever.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What can branch/line coverage from forge coverage reveal that 'all tests pass' doesn't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An untested revert branch, an unreached else, or a function only ever exercised on one code path. Pitfall: 100% line coverage doesn't mean every input combination or invariant is tested — coverage measures reached code, not correctness.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What's the difference between running a forge script with and without --broadcast?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Without --broadcast it's a dry-run simulation against a fork — nothing is sent. With --broadcast, every call between vm.startBroadcast()/stopBroadcast() becomes a real signed transaction. Pitfall: forgetting --broadcast means nothing deployed, and you won't notice unless you check for the expected address/tx hash.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a minimal forge script deploying a Counter with a constructor arg of 42.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function run() external { vm.startBroadcast(); new Counter(42); vm.stopBroadcast(); }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why must compiler settings match exactly for forge verify-contract to succeed, even when the source is 'the same'?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Verification recompiles your submitted source with the settings you give it and compares the resulting bytecode against on-chain bytecode — identical including the metadata hash is a 'full match', identical except that trailing hash is still accepted as a 'partial match', but a solc version, optimizer-runs, or EVM-version mismatch changes the executable bytecode itself and fails even a partial match. Pitfall: constructor arguments must be ABI-encoded exactly as deployed (cast abi-encode) — a wrong encoding also fails the match.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What breaks if a fresh clone of a Foundry repo skips `git submodule update --init` before `forge build`?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: lib/ directories exist as empty submodule placeholders with no source inside, so any import from a dependency fails to resolve. Pitfall: forge install pins a specific commit, not 'latest' — a submodule silently stays on that commit until you deliberately forge update it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does a line like `@openzeppelin/=lib/openzeppelin-contracts/` in remappings.txt do, and what does `forge remappings` show beyond what you wrote by hand?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It rewrites any import starting with @openzeppelin/ to resolve under lib/openzeppelin-contracts/. forge remappings prints the FULL resolved table, including entries auto-inferred from installed dependencies. Pitfall: a typo'd prefix fails silently as 'file not found', not as a remapping error.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a remappings.txt line mapping forge-std imports to lib/forge-std/src/.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: forge-std/=lib/forge-std/src/

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does installing a dependency with soldeer differ from forge install for a git submodule, in terms of where the dependency's version is recorded?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: soldeer writes a versioned [dependencies] entry directly into foundry.toml and stores the package under dependencies/ (registry-resolved, like npm/cargo); forge install adds a .gitmodules entry pinned to a git commit under lib/. Pitfall: mixing both in one project is fine, but remappings must still be correct for whichever mechanism placed a given package.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does FOUNDRY_PROFILE change which foundry.toml settings apply, and why give [profile.ci] more fuzz runs than [profile.default]?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: FOUNDRY_PROFILE=ci makes Foundry read [profile.ci], falling back to [profile.default] for any key it doesn't override. Fewer runs locally means fast iteration; more runs in CI means a fuller check before merge, without changing test code. Pitfall: a key missing from [profile.ci] silently inherits from [profile.default] — an incomplete profile isn't an error, just a partial override.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a foundry.toml block giving the ci profile 1024 fuzz runs.
proposedPrompts.answerHint:
[profile.ci]
fuzz = { runs = 1024 }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What class of bug can Slither/Aderyn catch that a passing test suite might miss, and why?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Static analyzers flag patterns like reentrancy-prone external calls before state updates, unchecked low-level call returns, or uninitialized state — by reading code structure, not executing it, so they catch a bug class even if no test happens to exercise that exact path. Pitfall: static analysis produces false positives routinely — triage findings, don't blindly 'fix' every warning.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does hardhat.config.ts declare, and what testing option does Hardhat 3 add that Hardhat 2 didn't have?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The Solidity compiler version/settings, source/test paths, and networks. Hardhat 3 adds first-class Foundry-compatible Solidity tests (.t.sol, forge-std style) alongside the original TypeScript test runner. Pitfall: both test styles still compile from ONE shared contracts/ tree — a config mistake there breaks both.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Complete Speedrun Ethereum challenges 0–2 (Simple NFT Example, Decentralized Staking App, Token Vendor).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Each challenge scaffolds a Scaffold-ETH 2 (Hardhat-based) project with a contract plus a Next.js frontend; deploy locally with Hardhat, pass the contract's own test suite, then follow the challenge's deploy/verify steps.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why write a TS integration test with viem in addition to a Foundry Solidity test for the same contract?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A TS test exercises the same client code (viem) a frontend or deploy script actually uses, catching ABI/typing mismatches and multi-contract wiring bugs a Solidity-only test wouldn't see. Pitfall: TS tests are slower per-call than Foundry's in-process Solidity tests — reserve them for integration/deployment concerns, not fine-grained unit/fuzz coverage.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a viem-based Hardhat TS test deploying a contract and asserting a read call.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: const counter = await viem.deployContract("Counter"); await counter.write.increment(); expect(await counter.read.count()).to.equal(1n);

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Ignition's deployment journal let you safely do that a plain imperative deploy script can't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Resume a partially-failed multi-contract deployment without re-deploying contracts that already succeeded, because Ignition tracks what's been deployed against a module's declared dependency graph. Pitfall: Ignition modules are declarative, so imperative control flow (loops/conditionals over deploys) doesn't work the way a hand-written script would.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a minimal Hardhat Ignition module deploying a Counter with a constructor arg of 0.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: import { buildModule } from "@nomicfoundation/hardhat-ignition/modules"; export default buildModule("Phase03", (m) => { const counter = m.contract("Counter", [0]); return { counter }; });

proposedPrompts.promptText: What's the difference between an edr-simulated network and an http network in Hardhat 3's config, and why keep RPC URLs as configuration variables?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: edr-simulated runs an in-memory local chain (optionally forking a real one); http points at a real JSON-RPC endpoint. Configuration variables keep secrets (RPC URLs, keys) out of the committed hardhat.config.ts. Pitfall: a forking network config still needs a valid url to fork from — omitting it silently breaks the fork.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does a Hardhat plugin actually add to a project, beyond 'more npm packages'?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: New CLI tasks, new config keys the loader validates, and extensions to the Hardhat Runtime Environment every task/script receives (e.g. a typed viem client). Pitfall: two plugins can extend the same HRE property or task name and conflict — check compatibility before stacking many at once.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Hardhat 3 actually read to resolve a remapped Solidity import, and what does it NOT parse directly?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Hardhat 3 loads its own remappings.txt files — found at the project root, in subdirectories, or bundled with an installed npm package — it does NOT parse foundry.toml. A project relying only on foundry.toml's [profile] remappings needs an equivalent remappings.txt for Hardhat to resolve the same import. Pitfall: assuming Hardhat 'just reads' foundry.toml leads to an import resolving under forge build but failing under npx hardhat build.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can a Foundry .t.sol test run unmodified under Hardhat's own test runner, without either tool 'owning' it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Hardhat 3 recognizes any test/ file or file ending .t.sol written against forge-std as a native Solidity test, so the identical file executes under both `forge test` and `npx hardhat test` — the split is by which runner you invoke, not by which tool a test 'belongs' to. Pitfall: Hardhat and Foundry can default to different solc versions/optimizer settings — keep compiler settings aligned or the two runs can subtly diverge.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: When to reach for Foundry vs Hardhat
proposedPrompts.promptText: Give the one-line decision rule for choosing Foundry vs Hardhat for a given task in this curriculum.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Foundry for fast iterative Solidity testing (unit/fuzz/invariant/gas/security work); Hardhat for TS-typed deployment pipelines (Ignition) and anything a frontend (viem/wagmi) will call the same way. Pitfall: 'always Foundry' or 'always Hardhat' is the wrong takeaway — most real repos deliberately use both for different jobs.
